choose_status: Choose a folder to preview its events.
busy_open: Reading the saved options, finding the date of every file, and calculating the event clusters…
busy_preview: Calculating the event clusters again with your options…
busy_apply_check: Checking the folder again and recalculating the event clusters, so the question shows exactly what will move…
busy_apply: Clusters are ready. Creating the event folders and moving the files into them…
busy_flatten_check: Looking for event folders to flatten. No clusters are calculated in this step…
busy_flatten: Moving the files out of the event folders and removing the empty folders…
busy_after_flatten: The files are back in the folder. Recalculating the event clusters for the preview…
busy_after_error: The move stopped. Recalculating the event clusters from what is on disk now…
placeholder_timeline: Choose a folder to see its events on a timeline.
placeholder_day: Click a day in the calendar or on the timeline.
safety_limits: Safety limits around the learned boundary
floor_hint: Pauses shorter than this stay in the same event, whatever the learned boundary says.
ceiling_hint: Pauses longer than this always start a new event.
years_frame: Which years count, and which stamp wins
limit_min_year_hint: A stamp before this year is ignored.
limit_max_year_hint: A stamp after this year is ignored.
limit_prec_clock_hint: Higher wins when one name also matches an epoch or a bare date.
limit_prec_epoch_hint: Priority of a Unix millisecond stamp.
limit_prec_date_hint: Priority of a date that has no time.
model_help: Read-only view of the learned fields in filenamecluster-model.json. The preview also writes the options from this tab under options in that file. This table does not edit either.
model_within: Typical pause inside an event, in hours.
model_between: Typical pause between events, in hours.
patterns_help: Each row is one regular expression. The built-in rules are already listed; use Add pattern for another. Clear an expression to turn that row off. A clock needs groups y, mo, d, h, mi and s (ms is optional). A day-month clock needs a, b, y, h and mi (s is optional). Unix milliseconds needs ms. A date needs y, mo and d.

groups_clock: y, mo, d, h, mi, s
groups_day_month: a, b, y, h, mi; optional s

about_what_body: File Name Cluster groups timestamped files in one folder into events. It uses the date and time written in each filename, or only picture, video, or PDF creation metadata when the name has none. Each event can then be moved into its own folder, numbered in chronological order.
about_how_body:
1. Click “Choose folder…” and pick the folder that holds the files.
2. The events appear right away: on the to-scale timeline at the top, in the calendar, and in the cluster list. Nothing has been moved yet.
3. Click a day in the calendar, or anywhere on the timeline, to see that day hour by hour with every file listed. Click a bar or a row in the cluster list to jump to that event.
4. The boundary between events is learned from the timestamps in this folder. A frequent photographer and an occasional one get different boundaries. If the filename has no timestamp, only picture, video, or PDF creation time is read. If that time cannot be read, the file is listed in the Skipped tab. Click “Update preview” after changing the safety limits.
5. Click “Apply clustering” to create the folders and move the files. You are asked to confirm first. The timeline, calendar, and cluster list stay as they are until you choose another folder.
6. Copy more files into the same folder later, then click “Update preview”. Files already in event folders are included. A new file joins an existing event when the pause is short enough, or starts a new event when it is not. Apply then moves only the files that need a different folder, and renames an event folder whose times changed.
7. Click “Flatten clustering” to move those files back into the chosen folder and remove the event folders. Other subfolders are left alone.
8. Use the Language menu to show this window in English, Hindi, Marathi, German, French, Japanese, or Korean.
about_views_body:
Timeline: one bar per event, drawn to scale, with a tick for every file underneath. Use −, + and Fit, or Ctrl/Cmd with the mouse wheel, to zoom. The plain wheel scrolls sideways.
Calendar: days with files are coloured and show the event number (#) and file count. Paler days sit inside a multi-day event but have no files. ◀ and ▶ move one month; ◀◀ and ▶▶ jump to the previous or next month that has files.
Day detail: the chosen day from 00:00 to 24:00, with its files and the event each belongs to.
Cluster list: click # to sort by event number, or Files to sort by how many files each event holds. Click the same heading again to reverse the order; ↑ and ↓ show the direction. The events with the most files are the major ones, so sorting Files downward brings those to the top.
Double-click the orange or yellow event in the calendar, on a timeline, or in the cluster list to open its folder in a new file-manager window. If that folder has not been created yet, you are told so.
Double-click a file in the Day detail table to open it with the application your system uses for that kind of file.
about_names_body:
An event on one calendar day:  1 24-11-2015 10.01.25 to 18.50.08
An event across several days:  2 09-11-2015 20.49.41 to 12-11-2015 10.24.42
The leading number keeps the folders in chronological order.
about_files_body:
Files sitting directly in the chosen folder are clustered, and so are files already inside event folders from an earlier Apply. Other subfolders are never entered. When a name has no timestamp, only capture time from a recognised picture or video, or CreationDate from a PDF, is read. If that also cannot be read, the file stays where it is and is listed in the Skipped tab. Existing files are never overwritten.
Recognised names include IMG_20240101_101500.jpg, VID_20240101_101500.mp4, IMG-20240101-WA0001.jpg and VID-20240101-WA0001.mp4 (taken as midnight), PANO_…, 20240101101500123.jpg, Screenshot_2024-01-01-10-15-00.png, CamScanner 01-02-2024 10.15.pdf and 13-digit Unix millisecond stamps.
about_options_body:
The app fits two patterns to the pauses in the chosen folder: short pauses inside an event, and long pauses between events. The boundary is where a pause looks more like the long pattern. It is learned again for every folder, from timestamps only. If the filename has no timestamp, only picture, video, or PDF creation time is read. If that time cannot be read, the file is listed in the Skipped tab.
Never split before (default 3 h) and always split after (default 720 h) are safety limits around that learned boundary.
The learned boundary is saved in filenamecluster-model.json in the chosen folder, next to the files, where you can open it. The Options tab shows the learned fields of that file in a read-only table: within_hours, between_hours, boundary_hours, and separated. It is reused when a later batch is too small to fit a new one.
Minimum and maximum year (defaults 1990 and 2100): a stamp outside this window is ignored.
Clock, epoch and date priority (defaults 30, 20 and 10): when one filename matches more than one pattern, the higher number wins. A tie keeps the match that starts earlier in the name.
Filename patterns: the regular expressions used to read a time from a name. They start out as rows in the table. Add a row for another kind of name, clear an expression to turn that rule off, or replace it. A clock pattern needs the groups y, mo, d, h, mi and s. The day-month clock needs a, b, y, h and mi. Unix milliseconds needs ms. A date needs y, mo and d. Then click “Update preview”.
The values from this tab are saved in that same file under options, beside learned. Choosing the folder loads those saved options over the built-in defaults. The learned boundary is still fitted and reused exactly as before.
about_regex_body:
A filename pattern is a small recipe. It tells the app which digits in the file name are the date, and which digits are the time.

The app looks only at the file name. It does not look at the folder.

Letters may sit around the digits. IMG_ and .jpg are fine. The date can be in the middle of the name. The search is called finditer. That means the recipe may match anywhere, and it may match more than once. It does not have to describe the whole name.

Each row on the Options tab is one recipe. A blank recipe turns that row off. The app skips it.
about_regex_marks_body:
Read a recipe from left to right. Each mark means one small thing.

\d means one digit. A digit is 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, or 9.
\d{{4}} means exactly four digits in a row. \d{{2}} means exactly two. \d{{1,2}} means one digit or two digits. \d{{1,3}} means one, two, or three. \d{{13}} means exactly thirteen.

(?P<y>...) means: remember the digits inside, and call them y. The letters between < and > are the name. Only the names in the next section are understood. Parentheses with no ?P<name> do not become a time. They only hold marks together.

(?<!\d) means: do not start if the character just before is a digit.
(?!\d) means: do not finish if the next character is a digit.
Together they stop the app from cutting a long number in half. A 17-digit clock is not also read as a shorter clock.

[_-] means one underscore or one dash.
[.:] means one dot or one colon.
(?:...) holds marks together and does not give them a name.
A ? just after a group means that group may be missing.
\s+ means one or more spaces.

Some marks are special. When you want the character itself, put a backslash in front. Those characters are . ^ $ * + ? ( ) [ ] {{ }} | and the backslash. A real dot is often written as [.] or as a backslash and a dot. A dash between two numbers can stay a plain dash, because there it is not inside [ ].
about_regex_kinds_body:
The names inside (?P<name>...) choose the kind of time. You must use exactly the names for one kind. An extra name, or a missing required name, makes that row invalid. Update preview then stays where it was, and the status line names the row.

1. Clock. You must name y, mo, d, h, mi, and s. You may also name ms. No other names.
y is the year. mo is the month, from 1 to 12. d is the day. h is the hour, from 0 to 23. mi is the minute. s is the second.
ms is a piece of a second. One digit is tenths. Two digits are hundredths. Three digits are milliseconds. Any other length is skipped for that match.
This kind uses Clock priority.

2. Day and month beside the year. You must name a, b, y, h, and mi. You may also name s. If s is missing, the second is 0. No other names.
a and b are the two numbers next to the year. The app first tries day then month. If that date cannot exist, it tries month then day. So both 11-21-2024 and 21-11-2024 can work.
This kind uses the same Clock priority.

3. Unix milliseconds. The only name is ms. The digits count milliseconds since 1 January 1970 UTC. The app turns them into the local time of this computer, so they line up with camera names.
This kind uses Epoch priority.

4. Date only. You must name y, mo, and d. No other names. The time is midnight on that day.
This kind uses Date priority.

Month 13, hour 25, and 31 February are not real. The app skips them. A year before Minimum year or after Maximum year is skipped too. Those start at 1990 and 2100.

If two recipes both find a time in one name, the bigger priority wins. Clock starts at 30. Epoch starts at 20. Date starts at 10. If they tie, the match that starts earlier in the name wins.
about_regex_camera_body:
The file name is IMG_20240101_101500.jpg.

This is the compact-clock recipe. Its key is clock_compact_sep.

(?<!\d)(?P<y>\d{{4}})(?P<mo>\d{{2}})(?P<d>\d{{2}})[_-](?P<h>\d{{2}})(?P<mi>\d{{2}})(?P<s>\d{{2}})(?P<ms>\d{{1,3}})?(?!\d)

Read the name from the left, one mark at a time.

1. IMG_ is letters and an underscore. The recipe is waiting for digits, so it walks past IMG_.
2. The digits start at 20240101_101500. The character just before 2 is _. That is not a digit, so (?<!\d) says yes, start here.
3. (?P<y>\d{{4}}) takes the next four digits, 2024, and names them y. The year is 2024.
4. (?P<mo>\d{{2}}) takes 01 and names them mo. The month is 1. That is January.
5. (?P<d>\d{{2}}) takes 01 and names them d. The day is 1.
6. [_-] needs one underscore or one dash. The next character is _. That fits.
7. (?P<h>\d{{2}}) takes 10. The hour is 10.
8. (?P<mi>\d{{2}}) takes 15. The minute is 15.
9. (?P<s>\d{{2}}) takes 00. The second is 0.
10. (?P<ms>\d{{1,3}})? would take one, two, or three more digits for a fraction of a second. The ? means this part may be missing. The next character is a dot, not a digit, so there is no fraction.
11. (?!\d) checks the next character. It is a dot, not a digit, so the match may end.

The clock is 1 January 2024 at 10:15:00.
about_regex_scan_body:
The file name is CamScanner 11-21-2024 12.22.jpg.

This is the day-month recipe. Its key is numeric_date.

(?<!\d)(?P<a>\d{{1,2}})-(?P<b>\d{{1,2}})-(?P<y>\d{{4}})\s+(?P<h>\d{{2}})[.:](?P<mi>\d{{2}})(?:[.:](?P<s>\d{{2}}))?

1. CamScanner and the space are not digits. The recipe walks past them.
2. The character before 11 is a space, not a digit, so it may start.
3. (?P<a>\d{{1,2}}) takes 11 and names it a. One or two digits are allowed. Here there are two.
4. The next character must be a dash. It is.
5. (?P<b>\d{{1,2}}) takes 21 and names it b.
6. Another dash.
7. (?P<y>\d{{4}}) takes 2024. The year is 2024.
8. \s+ takes the space after the year. That means one or more spaces.
9. (?P<h>\d{{2}}) takes 12. The hour is 12.
10. [.:] takes a dot or a colon. Here it is a dot.
11. (?P<mi>\d{{2}}) takes 22. The minute is 22.
12. The last part, (?:[.:](?P<s>\d{{2}}))?, would be a dot or a colon and then two digits for the seconds. The ? means it may be missing. After 22 comes .jpg. j is not a digit, so the seconds are left out. The second is 0.

Now the app has two numbers beside the year: a is 11 and b is 21. It tries them in two orders.

First it tries day then month: day 11, month 21. There is no month 21, so that reading is thrown away.

Then it tries month then day: month 11, day 21. That date exists. It is 21 November 2024.

The clock is 21 November 2024 at 12:22:00.
about_regex_table_body:
Double-click a description or a recipe to change it. Enter keeps the change. Escape throws it away.

Add pattern adds a row. Remove pattern deletes the selected row. Update preview checks every row that is not blank.

The built-in rows keep a fixed key: clock_separated, clock_compact_sep, clock_compact_17, clock_compact_14, numeric_date, epoch_ms, and date_only. A row you add has an empty key.

Other names the built-in rows already understand:
2024-01-01-10-15-00 is a dashed clock. Year, month, day, hour, minute, and second, with dashes between them. Three millisecond digits may follow one more dash.
20240101101500123 is seventeen digits: date, time, and milliseconds, and the next character is not a digit.
20240101101500 is fourteen digits: date and time, and the next character is not a digit, so the seventeen-digit form is left to its own row.
img1462863402727.jpg is exactly thirteen digits. Those are Unix milliseconds.
IMG-20240101-WA0001.jpg is a date only. The time is midnight. A full clock in the same name wins, because Clock priority is higher than Date priority.

A new name such as hour is not read. Digits with no ?P<name> are not a time. To turn a built-in row off without deleting it, clear the recipe. Restore defaults puts the built-in recipes, the safety limits, the year window, and the priorities back.

These recipes only read the clock. They do not decide where one event ends. That is still learned from the pauses between clocks. Every row is saved under options, beside learned, so the folder reopens with the same recipes.
about_logging_body:
The application writes a text log while it runs. Each line starts with a timestamp in the form YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.mmm and the process id as pid=N. CALL is written just before a function runs, ENTER when that function begins, and EXIT when it returns. EVENT marks a key step such as choosing a folder, loading or saving the model, updating the preview, applying clustering, flattening, or restoring defaults. DETAIL records a decision inside a function: which clock was read from a name, whether a pause split an event, each fit iteration, a reused or fallback boundary, and each file moved or left in place. The Options tab includes Write application log. It is off when the app opens. Turning it on writes new lines until you turn it off again.
The file is stored where this operating system keeps application logs. On macOS that file is ~/Library/Logs/filenamecluster/filenamecluster.log. On Windows it is %LOCALAPPDATA%/filenamecluster/Logs/filenamecluster.log. On Linux it is $XDG_STATE_HOME/filenamecluster/filenamecluster.log, or ~/.local/state/filenamecluster/filenamecluster.log when XDG_STATE_HOME is unset.
On this computer the log file is {path}.
